visual.description: Opens with a visual provocation synced to voiceover: 0–2s a chips bag visibly shrinks (spring animation, 20 frames), 2–4s a coffee can shrinks alongside a weight counter ticking down '16 oz → 10 oz'. At ~5s, title 'Shrinkflation Decoded' fades in Montserrat ExtraBold 72px, Accent Cream — then fades out by ~8s. By ~10s the shrink props dissolve and 6 product icons (eggs, coffee, chips, milk, peanut butter, ice cream) emerge at a starting line, all at RUPI = 1.0 baseline. Baseline reference line pulses gently in Sage Silver. Background: solid #1A1B22 with dot grid at 10% opacity.

scenes.notes: HOOK VISUAL-FIRST: First 5 seconds must grab attention visually. 0–2s: chips bag shrink micro-animation (spring stiffness 120, damping 18, 20 frames). 2–4s: coffee can shrink with weight counter (JetBrains Mono tnum, count from 16→10). These sync with voiceover 'bag of chips is smaller' and 'coffee can lost a third.' Title fade-in at ~5s with muted easing (bezier 0.33,1,0.68,1) over 30 frames — NOT at 0s. Title fades out by ~8s. Product icons stagger in at 10-frame intervals starting ~10s. Baseline reference line (RUPI = 1.0) pulses subtly — 2s cycle, opacity 0.6→1.0→0.6. Film grain overlay 3%.
scenes.voiceover: Your bag of chips is smaller. Your coffee can lost a third of its weight. Everyone says groceries are more expensive. <break time="500ms"/> But when you measure the actual price per unit against median wages... four out of six common grocery products cost LESS of your paycheck today than they did in the year two thousand.

visual.description: Race chart preview flash — a 2-second animation showing 4 of 6 lines dipping below the RUPI 1.0 baseline (green zone) and 2 lines shooting above (red zone). This is a rapid preview of the final chart state to create intrigue. Then the chart blurs/fades and text appears: 'So why doesn't it feel that way?' in Montserrat Bold 48px, centered.

textOverlay.text: So why doesn't it feel that way?

dataChart.questionText: So why doesn't it feel that way?

scenes.notes: Short dramatic beat. The 1000ms leading break gives visual time to transition. Flash the end-state chart for 2 seconds (blurred, quick), then crossfade to the question text. The question hangs for 3 seconds. This is the hook's punchline — leave it breathing. Film grain 3%.
scenes.voiceover: <break time="1000ms"/> The data says you're winning. <break time="500ms"/> So why doesn't it feel that way?

visual.description: Split comparison card. Left side: '2000' header — '$572/week' (JetBrains Mono, Muted Pink), 'Eggs: $0.91/dozen' below. Right side: '2025' header — '$1,206/week' (JetBrains Mono, Muted Blue), 'Eggs: $4.25/dozen'. Thin vertical divider in Sage Silver. Numbers animate in with spring counters. At the 500ms break, the comparison fades and the RUPI formula builds: 'Price Growth ÷ Wage Growth = RUPI' — each term animates in sequence. BLS logo watermark bottom-right, small, at 30% opacity.

scenes.notes: This is the educational foundation scene. The concrete wage/egg comparison makes it tangible before introducing the abstract formula. Phase 1 (comparison card) holds for ~20s, then phase 2 (formula) builds for the remaining ~19s. Numbers use JetBrains Mono with tabular figures. Spring animation for counter: stiffness 100, damping 20. BLS source footnote in Inter 14px, Sage Silver, bottom-right.
scenes.voiceover: Imagine you earned five hundred seventy-two dollars a week in two thousand. A dozen eggs cost ninety-one cents. Today you earn twelve hundred — but eggs cost four twenty-five. Did eggs get more expensive... or did your paycheck grow faster? <break time="500ms"/> That's the question behind what we call the Real Unit Price Index — RUPI. Take twenty-five years of Bureau of Labor Statistics prices — per pound, per gallon, per dozen — and divide each product's price growth by median wage growth.

visual.description: RUPI baseline reference diagram. Horizontal line at RUPI = 1.0 (Sage Silver). Above the line: red-tinted zone with upward arrow and label 'More expensive relative to wages' (Muted Red #E06070). Below the line: green-tinted zone with downward arrow and label 'Cheaper relative to wages' (Muted Green #5BBF8C). At the line: label '= Same as 2000' (Accent Cream). Clean, minimal — this is the visual legend for the rest of the video.

scenes.notes: Critical visual legend. This diagram will be referenced visually throughout. Keep it extremely clean — no chart data yet, just the conceptual framework. Labels animate in with 10-frame stagger: first the baseline, then above zone, then below zone. Each zone has a subtle gradient fill (15% opacity). This scene is brief but essential for comprehension.
scenes.voiceover: <break time="500ms"/> One means a product costs the same share of your paycheck as in two thousand. Above one — it's taking a bigger bite. Below one — wages won.

visual.description: Shrinkflation explanation animation. A coffee can (stylized, minimal, Muted Pink fill) starts at '16 oz' — then visually shrinks to '10 oz' while the price tag next to it stays fixed at '$4.99'. After the shrink, a 'per pound' price counter animates upward: '$4.99/lb → $7.99/lb' in JetBrains Mono, Muted Red. Small BLS logo with text 'BLS tracks per-unit price' fades in below. Background: solid #1A1B22.

scenes.notes: This is a preemptive objection handler — addresses the viewer's likely skepticism before the race starts. The coffee can animation should feel smooth: shrink over 45 frames using spring (stiffness 100, damping 20). The price counter should use the number interpolation animation (30 frames). The BLS attribution should be subtle — Inter 16px, Sage Silver. The key visual moment is when the per-pound price ticks up despite the sticker price staying the same.
scenes.voiceover: <break time="500ms"/> Now — a common objection. If companies are shrinking packages, doesn't that hide inflation? Actually, the BLS already accounts for this. When your coffee can shrinks from sixteen ounces to ten at the same sticker price, BLS records that as a price INCREASE per pound. Shrinkflation is already baked into the numbers you're about to see.

visual.description: Race start lineup. The full race chart appears for the first time — X-axis: 2000–2025 (JetBrains Mono), Y-axis: RUPI scale. Six colored dots clustered at the starting position (Year 2000, RUPI 1.0), each with a small product icon label. Product labels stagger in. Baseline reference line prominent. Dot grid background active. At 'Let the race begin' — a subtle glow/pulse on the starting dots.

scenes.notes: Dramatic pause before the race. The 500ms break at the start gives time for the chart to establish. The 1000ms break after 'one point zero' is where the dots should pulse/glow — building anticipation. At 'Let the race begin' the dots should brighten momentarily. LINE STYLES: Defined in sharedComponents.raceChart.products. Only 2 vivid colors (Pink=Eggs, Blue=Coffee); remaining 4 use Accent Cream at varying opacity/dash patterns for differentiation without violating brand guide's 2-color max.
scenes.voiceover: <break time="500ms"/> Six products. All starting at one point zero. <break time="1000ms"/> Let the race begin.

visual.description: Race chart animates 2000→2009. Chapter marker 'ACT 1: THE DIVERGENCE' fades in top-left in Montserrat Bold 36px, then fades to 20% opacity. All 6 lines begin moving from the starting position. Eggs (Muted Pink, thick line) immediately breaks upward — reaching ~1.31 by 2004, then surging to ~1.73 by 2008. At year 2001, a brief 'how to read' overlay appears for 3 seconds: arrow up = 'More expensive relative to wages', arrow down = 'Cheaper', horizontal = 'Same as 2000'. Egg RUPI value tooltip tracks the line: '1.31' at 2004, '1.73' at 2008. Other lines visible but not highlighted.

scenes.notes: The race begins. Use strokeDashoffset reveal for line animation, left-to-right, synchronized with the voiceover timeline. The 'how to read' overlay at 2001 should be semi-transparent (surface color bg), appear for exactly 3 seconds, then fade. Eggs should be the ONLY prominently colored line (Muted Pink, 3px). Other lines in Sage Silver or Accent Cream at 60% opacity, 1.5px. Egg line animation: spring stiffness 100, damping 20 for the vertical movement. Show year marker advancing along x-axis as chart animates.
scenes.voiceover: Two thousand to two thousand nine. <break time="500ms"/> Right away, eggs break from the pack. An avian flu scare in two thousand three pushes them up. By two thousand four, they're already about thirty percent above the baseline — more of your paycheck for the same dozen. Then a global commodity surge in two thousand seven and eight drives them higher. By two thousand eight, eggs are the clear outlier — nearly seventy-five percent more of your weekly wage than they cost in two thousand.

visual.description: Same race chart, now highlighting coffee line (Muted Blue, thick). Eggs line remains visible but dimmed to 40% opacity. Coffee drifts from 1.0 down to ~0.74 by 2004. A tooltip tracks the coffee line showing the RUPI value. Small annotation near the coffee line at 2004: '~25% cheaper'. Green zone below baseline subtly glows as coffee enters it.

scenes.notes: Visual focus shift from eggs to coffee. The chart doesn't reset — it continues from scene-007's state but shifts emphasis. Coffee line becomes Muted Blue 3px, eggs dims to 40% opacity. The green zone below 1.0 should have a subtle glow pulse when coffee enters it. Other product lines remain as thin background lines. This creates contrast with the egg story.
scenes.voiceover: <break time="500ms"/> Coffee does the opposite. It drifts steadily downward through the early two thousands. By two thousand four, a pound of ground roast takes about a quarter less of your paycheck than it did at the start of the decade. Coffee kept getting cheaper.

visual.description: Same race chart — all 6 lines at equal visual weight. The middle 4 products (chips, milk, peanut butter, ice cream) are now highlighted with slightly brighter opacity, hovering around the 1.0 baseline (all between ~0.85 and ~1.07). At 2008, a brief event marker appears: '2008: Financial Crisis' in Accent Cream, small. Milk and chips briefly spike above 1.0 in 2008, then settle back by 2009. Eggs remain elevated. Coffee remains low.

scenes.notes: Now showing the 'boring middle' — which is actually the story of wages keeping pace. All product lines visible at moderate opacity. The financial crisis event marker should appear as a vertical dashed line at 2008 with label. The brief surge of milk/chips above 1.0 should be visible but not overemphasized — they return below by 2009. This sets up the 'everything is fine' narrative that will be complicated later. Note: Chips is the exception — it stayed slightly above 1.0 in 2009 (1.056). The voiceover hedges with 'most products'. Consider dimming the chips line slightly during 2009 to avoid viewer confusion, or adding a brief tooltip annotation.
scenes.voiceover: <break time="500ms"/> Chips, milk, peanut butter, ice cream — they all hover near the baseline. Wages are roughly keeping pace. Nothing dramatic. Nothing alarming. <break time="500ms"/> Then two thousand eight — the financial crisis. Milk and chips push briefly above one as commodity prices surge, but by two thousand nine, most products settle back down.

visual.description: Race chart background at 30% opacity — two shrinkflation annotation overlays appear on the chart near 2009. Annotation 1: 'Häagen-Dazs: 16 → 14 oz' with a small ice cream container icon that shrinks. Annotation 2: 'Skippy: 18 → 16.3 oz' with a peanut butter jar icon showing the indent. Each annotation has an arrow pointing to its product's line on the chart. Price tag overlay: '$3.99' in JetBrains Mono stays static while the package visually shrinks. Callout box: 'BLS records this as a price increase per unit.'

scenes.notes: First major shrinkflation showcase. The chart pauses at 2009 and the annotations overlay ON TOP of the chart — keeping the race context visible. The shrink animations should be smooth springs (stiffness 80, damping 18). The $3.99 price tag is the psychological anchor — it should be prominent, JetBrains Mono 36px, Accent Cream. The 'deeper indent' for Skippy is a nice detail — if feasible, show a side-view jar silhouette with the bottom dimple growing. Annotations should stagger in: Häagen-Dazs first (10-frame stagger), then Skippy.
scenes.voiceover: <break time="500ms"/> And behind the scenes — something quieter is happening. Häagen-Dazs shrinks its container from sixteen to fourteen ounces. Skippy redesigns its peanut butter jar — same height, deeper indent in the bottom — dropping from eighteen to sixteen point three ounces. <break time="500ms"/> Why? Because three ninety-nine is a magic number. Consumers notice when a price crosses four dollars. They don't notice when two ounces disappear. The BLS tracks price per unit, so the shrinkage shows up in the data. But the sticker price at the register? That barely moved.

visual.description: Race chart continues from 2009 into 2010–2019. Chapter marker 'ACT 2: THE QUIET DECADE' fades in top-left (Montserrat Bold 36px), then fades to 20%. Coffee line (Muted Blue) spikes above 1.0 in 2011 (RUPI ~1.14) and 2012 (~1.22), then falls back. Eggs line (Muted Pink) is volatile — dramatic peak in 2015 (RUPI ~1.93), then crash to ~1.07 by 2017. Event marker at 2015: 'Avian Flu Outbreak'. Both highlighted products get value tooltips at key points.

scenes.notes: The decade starts with two volatile products. Coffee and eggs both get 3px highlighted lines. The other 4 products should be visible but dim. The 2015 egg spike is dramatic — nearly 2.0 — make sure the Y-axis scale accommodates this. The egg crash from 1.93 to 1.07 should be visually rapid (compressed timeline animation). Coffee's brief excursion above 1.0 should be clearly visible — use a small callout when it crosses the baseline.
scenes.voiceover: The twenty-tens. The quiet decade. <break time="500ms"/> Coffee spikes above one in twenty eleven and twelve — a global commodity boom — then falls back below. It would stay below one for years. Eggs remain volatile. The twenty fifteen avian flu outbreak pushes them nearly twice as expensive as the baseline — then they crash back down by twenty seventeen.

visual.description: Same race chart, focus shifts to the bottom 4 products. Eggs and coffee dim to 30% opacity. The 4 remaining lines (chips, milk, peanut butter, ice cream) are highlighted — all clearly below the 1.0 baseline and trending downward. Each line gets a subtle trailing glow in green (#5BBF8C at 10% opacity) as it sinks deeper into the green zone. Product names label each line at their 2019 position. The green zone below 1.0 has a faint pulse.

scenes.notes: The 'quiet' visual. The downward drift should feel gentle and persistent — not dramatic. Use the slow strokeDashoffset reveal. Each product name should fade in near its line as the voice mentions it (10-frame stagger between products). The green zone glow reinforces 'this is good news'. Peanut butter is the lowest — label it prominently. This scene creates the false sense of security that Act 3 will shatter.
scenes.voiceover: <break time="500ms"/> But look at the rest of the field. They're drifting down. Slowly. Steadily. No single dramatic moment — just a gradual slide. Peanut butter. Milk. Chips. Ice cream. All sinking below one. Wages growing just a little faster than these prices, year after year.

visual.description: Race chart freezes at 2019. All 6 lines visible — ALL below the 1.0 baseline. A subtle annotation: '2019: All below 1.0' appears centered below the chart title. The 1000ms break at the end is a dramatic pause — the chart holds static with a slight vignette darkening at the edges, creating a 'false ending' feeling. Small text at bottom: 'Wages: +60% since 2000 | Food prices: held relatively flat.' Source footnote: 'BLS, FRED.'

scenes.notes: The false happy ending. This scene should feel conclusive — as if the video could end here. The vignette darkening at the edges during the 1000ms pause creates unease. All lines below 1.0 is the visual proof of 'wages won'. But the 1000ms dramatic pause signals to the viewer that something is about to change. Don't rush this — let the chart breathe. Even eggs dipped below 1.0 in 2019 (0.957). Note: the voiceover says 'every product sits below' — verify this matches 2019 wage-RUPI data.
scenes.voiceover: <break time="500ms"/> Why did this happen? The post-recovery economy. Unemployment fell. Labor markets tightened, especially after twenty sixteen. Wages started climbing — not dramatically, but persistently. And food commodity prices stayed relatively flat. <break time="500ms"/> By twenty nineteen, every product sits below the baseline — most of them well below it. The chart says things are getting better. It looks like the story has a happy ending. <break time="1000ms"/>

visual.description: FULL-SCREEN pattern interrupt — NO race chart on screen. Two before/after split cards stacked vertically. Top card: Doritos — left side shows '12 oz' bag (full-size icon), right side shows '9.25 oz' bag (visibly smaller icon). A red '-23%' badge animates in between them (spring, 15 frames). Bottom card: Folgers — left '16 oz' can, right '10.3 oz' can, '-36%' badge. Cards use surface background rgba(255,255,255,0.06) with border. Brand names in Inter 20px Accent Cream, weights in JetBrains Mono 28px. At voiceover mention of BLS stat, a callout card fades in at bottom: 'Snack food downsizing: 2.64% cumulative (2015–2019)' in JetBrains Mono 18px on surface card. This scene deliberately breaks from the chart to give the viewer's eyes a reset before the skimpflation concept scene.

scenes.notes: PATTERN INTERRUPT: This scene deliberately exits the race chart entirely. The viewer has been staring at the chart since scene 006 (~3.5 minutes). Full-screen before/after split cards break visual monotony. Shrink animations should be dramatic — spring stiffness 100, damping 20. The -23% and -36% badges animate in with a slight bounce. BLS stat card uses surface background. Voiceover says 'reportedly' and 'according to consumer tracking' — these are hedged claims (⚠️ unverified in research). After this scene, viewer returns to chart context in scene 015.
scenes.voiceover: Except — look at the shelf, not the chart. On the chart, chips sit just below the line — barely cheaper per ounce. But on the shelf, a standard Doritos bag reportedly shrank from twelve ounces to nine and a quarter. Twenty-three percent less product. Folgers, according to consumer tracking, went from a full one-pound can to ten point three ounces — thirty-six percent less coffee in the same-looking can. <break time="500ms"/> According to the BLS, the snack food category alone saw a cumulative two point six four percent price impact from downsizing between twenty fifteen and twenty nineteen. The price per ounce held steady. The package just got smaller. <break time="500ms"/>

visual.description: Phase 1 (~30s): Skimpflation concept visual. Three identical product cards side by side — same package icon, same size label, same price tag. But a subtle indicator shows degrading quality: stars/quality bar going from 5→4→3. Text label: 'SKIMPFLATION' in Montserrat Bold 48px, Muted Pink, centered above. Below: 'Same package. Cheaper ingredients. No data series.' in Inter 20px, Accent Cream. Phase 2 (~25s): Transition back to the race chart at 2019 showing the downward-drifting lines — now with a subtle question mark overlay at 30% opacity, suggesting the data may not tell the full story. Phase 3 (~15s): Chart holds still. 'The lines are drifting down. Everything looks calm.' — ominous still frame before Act 3.

textOverlay.title: SKIMPFLATION
textOverlay.subtitle: Same package. Cheaper ingredients. No data series.

dataChart.title: SKIMPFLATION
dataChart.subtitle: Same package. Cheaper ingredients. No data series.

scenes.notes: Longest scene in Act 2 — 70 seconds. Needs clear phase transitions to avoid visual monotony. Phase 1 (skimpflation concept, 0–30s) uses the Remotion component style — no chart, just clean graphic design. Phase 2 (30–55s) transitions BACK to the race chart — crossfade over 8 frames. Phase 3 (55–69.67s) is the ominous hold. The 1000ms break before the final sentence is where the question mark overlay should pulse. The final line 'Everything looks calm' should feel unsettling — a calm before the storm. Film grain 3%.
scenes.voiceover: And there's one more thing the data can't capture. Skimpflation. Same package, same size, same price — but cheaper ingredients. Thinner chips. Waterier ice cream. Less cocoa in the chocolate. Unlike shrinkflation, there's no government data series for this. No BLS measurement. It's real — economists acknowledge it — but it lives in the gap between what statistics can track and what your taste buds notice. <break time="500ms"/> If you were shopping during this decade, it probably didn't FEEL like things were getting cheaper. And in one sense, they weren't — per trip to the store. You were buying the same number of packages, paying roughly the same at checkout, getting less in the bag each time, and sometimes getting a lesser product too. The per-unit math works out. The grocery receipt doesn't care about per-unit math. <break time="1000ms"/> The lines are drifting down. Everything looks calm.

visual.description: Race chart continues into 2020. Chapter marker: 'ACT 3: THE RECKONING' fades in (Montserrat Bold 36px). All 6 lines dip downward at 2020 — a dramatic synchronized drop. COVID annotation callout: a bordered card overlaid on the chart at 2020 with text 'COVID Wage Anomaly: Median jumped as lower-wage workers lost jobs. Not a real improvement.' Card uses surface background, Accent Cream text, Inter 16px. Red exclamation icon. The dip is visually striking — from various 2019 positions, all lines drop ~10-15% simultaneously.

eventMarker.title: COVID Wage Anomaly
eventMarker.text: Median jumped as lower-wage workers lost jobs. Not a real improvement.

eventMarker.title: COVID Wage Anomaly
eventMarker.text: Median jumped as lower-wage workers lost jobs. Not a real improvement.

scenes.notes: The COVID dip is one of the most deceptive moments in the data. The annotation card is ESSENTIAL — without it, viewers might think food actually got cheaper during COVID. The card should appear 2 seconds after the dip becomes visible, with a subtle bounce entrance (spring stiffness 80, damping 18). The warning icon should be in Muted Red. All 6 lines dropping simultaneously is visually dramatic — animate them dropping over 15 frames.
scenes.voiceover: Twenty twenty. <break time="500ms"/> A dip across the board. Every product appears to get cheaper overnight. But this isn't because food prices dropped. During COVID, lower-wage workers disproportionately lost their jobs — retail, hospitality, food service. The people who remained employed skewed higher-income. So the median wage jumped. Not because anyone got a raise. Because the composition of who was still working changed. <break time="500ms"/> The prices on the chart were real. The wage improvement was a statistical artifact.

visual.description: Race chart animation accelerates through 2021–2022. COVID annotation fades out. 2021: lines recover from the dip, mostly normalizing. 2022: dramatic upward movement. ALL lines rise visibly. Eggs (Muted Pink) spike sharply — from ~1.05 to ~1.71. Event marker at 2022: 'Inflation Surge + Avian Flu' in Muted Red text. The upward movement of all lines should feel urgent — faster animation than previous years. A subtle red tint washes over the chart background (5% opacity) as lines cross above 1.0. The 'moving UP' moment should synchronize with arrows appearing next to each line.

scenes.notes: This is the storm scene. The animation speed should notably increase compared to the 'quiet decade' — convey urgency. The red tint on the chart background is subtle but effective. Eggs shooting from ~1.0 to ~1.7 in a single year should be the most dramatic line movement in the video so far. The event marker should be larger than previous ones — this is a major event. Use 30-frame animation for the 2022 surge.
scenes.voiceover: <break time="500ms"/> By twenty twenty-one, workers return — and the median normalizes. Then twenty twenty-two. Inflation surges. Supply chains still broken. Energy costs cascading through every product. Eggs spike — avian flu again, this time the worst outbreak in American history. Tens of millions of birds culled. <break time="500ms"/> Everything on the chart rises. For the first time in years, the lines are moving UP.

visual.description: Race chart continues 2023–2025. Most lines stabilize or edge down — chips, milk, peanut butter, ice cream all settle back toward their positions. But eggs (Muted Pink, thickened to 4px) keep climbing: 2023 ~1.58, 2024 ~1.73, 2025 → 2.21. A dramatic RUPI counter next to the egg line counts up: '2.21×' in JetBrains Mono 40px, Muted Pink. The '2×' threshold crossing should trigger a brief flash. Coffee line (Muted Blue) crosses back above 1.0 in 2025 with a small crossing indicator. Brief text annotations near relevant lines: 'Avian flu' near eggs, 'Brazil drought' near coffee.

scenes.notes: Eggs are the dramatic outlier — the counter tracking the RUPI value creates tension as it climbs. When it crosses 2.0, flash the number briefly in Muted Red before returning to Muted Pink. The egg line should be the thickest in the video (4px) during this scene. Coffee crossing above 1.0 is secondary but important — show it with a small upward-arrow indicator at the crossing point. The stabilization of other products provides visual contrast to the egg explosion.
scenes.voiceover: <break time="500ms"/> Twenty twenty-three and twenty-four — most products stabilize or edge back down. But not eggs. Avian flu keeps returning. And by twenty twenty-five, eggs have more than doubled relative to the baseline. More than doubled. The chart shows you exactly how far. This isn't about shrinkflation or corporate strategy — it's biology. Disease. The egg market runs on chickens, and the chickens keep getting sick. <break time="500ms"/> Coffee crosses back above one in twenty twenty-five — the first time in over a decade. Drought in Brazil. Crop failures in Vietnam. A pound of coffee now takes a bigger slice of your paycheck than it did twenty-five years ago.

visual.description: Race chart freezes at 2025. Full 2000–2025 view. All 6 lines visible with final RUPI values labeled at their endpoints in JetBrains Mono: Eggs 2.21 (Muted Pink, above), Coffee 1.13 (Muted Blue, above), Chips 0.95 (below), Milk 0.69 (below), Peanut Butter 0.64 (below, labeled 'Biggest winner'), Ice Cream 0.72 (below). A clear visual divide: 2 lines above the red zone, 4 lines in the green zone. Running tally appears bottom-center: '4 of 6: Cheaper relative to wages' in Montserrat Bold 28px. The chart holds static for the final beats.

scenes.notes: The race conclusion under wage deflation. The 1000ms leading break gives the previous scene's energy time to settle. This should feel like a completed story — but it's not. The final RUPI values should be prominently labeled. Use JetBrains Mono with tabular figures so numbers align cleanly. Peanut Butter gets a special callout: 'Biggest winner' in Muted Green. The '4 of 6' tally should animate in with a subtle spring. Hold this frame for the full 32s — it needs time to breathe before the lens switch.
scenes.voiceover: <break time="1000ms"/> But when the chart freezes at twenty twenty-five... look at the full picture. Peanut butter — down more than a third from the baseline. The biggest winner for your wallet. Milk and ice cream — both well below one. Even chips, despite all the shrinkage, sit just below the line. <break time="500ms"/> Four out of six products. Cheaper relative to wages. After twenty-five years. After everything.

visual.description: Phase 1 (~6s): The frozen race chart from scene-019 holds. The '4 of 6' tally is visible. Phase 2 (~6s): Chart slowly darkens to 20% opacity. Large text fades in center: 'But cheaper… for whom?' in Montserrat Bold 64px, Accent Cream. The ellipsis after 'cheaper' should appear with a 500ms delay — a typographic pause. Phase 3 (~6s): The question text fades, replaced by: 'What if we change the ruler?' in Montserrat 36px. Below it, three ruler icons representing different deflators emerge: 'Median Wage ✓', 'CPI ?', 'Min Wage ?'

phase2.text: What if we change the ruler?

dataChart.rulerQuestion: What if we change the ruler?

scenes.notes: THE PIVOT MOMENT. This scene bridges the wage-deflated race chart and the lens switch reveal. The 'for whom?' text is the emotional hinge of the entire video. Let it breathe — the two 1000ms breaks mean 2 full seconds of visual pause. The text should be the ONLY thing on screen during phase 2 — dark background, large type, no distractions. The question mark after 'CPI' and 'Min Wage' in phase 3 creates anticipation. 8-frame crossfade between phases.
scenes.voiceover: Here is the twist. Four out of six products, cheaper relative to wages. <break time="1000ms"/> But cheaper... for whom? <break time="1000ms"/> That index used median wages — the middle of the income distribution. The typical worker. What if we change the ruler?

visual.description: The race chart re-animates with CPI deflator. A 'deflator' indicator in the top-right corner switches from 'MEDIAN WAGE' to 'CPI' with a slide animation. The same 6 product lines visibly shift UPWARD — this is the key visual: identical chart structure, but all lines move up. Chips crosses above 1.0 (0.947 → 1.067) — show crossing indicator. Coffee jumps (1.125 → 1.268). Eggs climb (2.210 → 2.490). New tally: '3 of 6: More expensive (CPI-adjusted)'. Side stat panel shows: 'Wages: +111% | CPI: +87%' explaining the gap. Final positions labeled with CPI-RUPI values.

scenes.notes: FIRST LENS SWITCH. The morph animation is crucial — viewers must see the SAME chart with the SAME data but different lines positions. Use smooth spring animation (stiffness 100, damping 20) over 60 frames for the line position shift. The deflator indicator top-right should be a persistent UI element that stays through scenes 021-025. Chips crossing above 1.0 is the key visual surprise — use a flash at the crossing point. The side stat panel (wage vs CPI growth) should be in a surface-color card, right side. 1200ms leading break gives time for the deflator switch animation.
scenes.voiceover: <break time="1200ms"/> Switch to the Consumer Price Index — CPI. This is the government's standard measure of inflation. It tracks roughly eighty thousand prices across the economy every month. When we use CPI instead of wages, we're asking a simpler question: did food prices outpace general inflation? <break time="500ms"/> The lines shift up. Chips crosses above one. Coffee jumps higher. Eggs climb further. Now three products cost more in inflation-adjusted terms than they did twenty-five years ago. <break time="500ms"/> Why the difference? Because median wages grew faster than inflation over this period — about a hundred and eleven percent versus eighty-seven percent. The median worker gained real purchasing power. That's a good thing. But it means the wage-deflated view is the OPTIMISTIC one.

visual.description: The deflator indicator switches from 'CPI' to 'FEDERAL MINIMUM WAGE' — this switch should feel heavier/more dramatic than the CPI switch. Lines begin to shift but the main visual focus is on the minimum wage context: A large counter appears center-screen: '$7.25/hr' in JetBrains Mono 72px, Muted Red. Below it: 'Unchanged since July 2009' in Inter 24px. A running ticker starts: '16 years, 8 months and counting…' in JetBrains Mono 20px, with the months incrementing in real-time style. Small stat: '~1.1 million workers at this rate'. The chart is dimmed to 40% during this context build — it will snap to full visibility in scene-023.

scenes.notes: EMOTIONAL CORE SETUP. This scene builds context before showing the devastating chart. The $7.25 counter should dominate the screen — it's the most important number in this section. The running ticker ('16 years, 8 months and counting') creates urgency. Use Muted Red for the $7.25 to convey the stagnation. The multiple breaks in the voiceover (1200+1000+500+500+500 = 3.7s of pauses) mean this scene has lots of breathing room — use it for visual emphasis. Don't rush the chart transformation — let the context sink in first.
scenes.voiceover: <break time="1200ms"/> Now switch to the federal minimum wage. <break time="1000ms"/> Seven dollars and twenty-five cents an hour. That's the federal minimum wage in the United States. It was set in July of two thousand nine. <break time="500ms"/> It hasn't changed since. Not once. Sixteen years. Through a pandemic. Through the worst inflation in forty years. Through everything. <break time="500ms"/> Roughly one point one million American workers earn exactly this amount. <break time="500ms"/> Millions more earn close to it.

visual.description: Phase 1 (~10s): The chart snaps to full opacity and lines JUMP upward with spring animation. Five of six lines are now above 1.0. Only peanut butter barely stays below. The red zone above 1.0 intensifies. Tally updates: '5 of 6: More expensive'. The $7.25 ticker persists in the corner. Phase 2 (~35s): A comparison card overlays the bottom portion of the chart. Left side: '2000' — clock icon showing '11 min' of work, egg icon, '$0.91', '$5.15/hr'. Right side: '2025' — clock icon showing '35 min' of work, same egg icon, '$4.25', '$7.25/hr'. The clock hands animate: left clock fills to 11 min mark, right clock fills to 35 min mark. '3×' multiplier pulses between them in JetBrains Mono 56px, Muted Red.

scenes.notes: THE GUT PUNCH. Phase 1 (the line jump) is the single most dramatic visual moment in the video. All lines should jump simultaneously over 45 frames using spring animation (stiffness 100, damping 20). The jump should feel PHYSICAL — like the chart just got hit. Phase 2 (the minutes-of-work comparison) makes the abstraction concrete. The clock icon animation: left clock fills quickly (11 min is small), right clock fills slowly (35 min is large) — the visual speed difference itself tells the story. The '3×' should pulse once in Muted Red. The $7.25 ticker continues in the corner throughout.
scenes.voiceover: <break time="500ms"/> Watch the lines. <break time="1000ms"/> Five of six products jump above one. The chart transforms. What looked like a story about affordability becomes a very different story. <break time="500ms"/> Eggs — a minimum wage worker now needs more than three times the work hours to buy a dozen compared to two thousand. Think about that concretely. In two thousand, a dozen eggs at ninety-one cents cost a minimum wage worker about eleven minutes of work. Today, at four twenty-five, it costs over thirty-five minutes. Same dozen eggs. Same job. Three times the effort.

visual.description: Race chart with minimum wage deflator — full view. The minutes-of-work overlay fades out. Each product line is now labeled with its min-wage RUPI at the 2025 endpoint: Eggs 3.31, Coffee 1.68, Chips 1.42, Milk 1.04, Ice Cream 1.08 — ALL in the red zone above 1.0. Peanut Butter 0.95 is the lone holdout in the green zone — highlighted with a small green badge: 'Last holdout'. The $7.25 ticker continues. Split summary card fades in at the bottom: Left: 'Median Worker: 4 of 6 cheaper' (Muted Green). Right: 'Min Wage Worker: 5 of 6 more expensive' (Muted Red). Thin divider between them.

scenes.notes: This is the conclusion of the minimum wage section — the emotional peak. As the voiceover lists 'Coffee. Chips. Milk. Ice cream.' — each product's label should flash briefly (10-frame stagger) to draw the eye. The peanut butter 'Last holdout' badge should feel poignant, not celebratory. The split summary card is the key takeaway — 'Same economy. Different experience.' The visual contrast between green (left) and red (right) tells the story at a glance. Hold this frame during the 1200ms break to let it sink in.
scenes.voiceover: <break time="500ms"/> Coffee. Chips. Milk. Ice cream. All above the line. Products that looked like bargains under median wages are now MORE expensive for anyone stuck at the federal floor. <break time="500ms"/> Only peanut butter stays below — barely. Just under one. The last holdout. <break time="1200ms"/> The median worker gained purchasing power over twenty-five years. The minimum wage worker lost it. Same economy. Same products. Same quarter century. A completely different experience depending on where you sit in the income distribution.

visual.description: The deflator indicator switches to 'GOLD'. All 6 lines collapse dramatically downward — from their minimum-wage positions high above 1.0, they plummet toward zero. Every single line ends well below 1.0 (all between 0.107 and 0.371). The visual effect should be striking: the chart that just showed catastrophe now shows everything as a bargain. Brief tally: '0 of 6: More expensive'. The animation should feel surreal — too good to be true. A small footnote appears: 'Gold: +1,155% since 2000'. The final line 'But no one buys eggs with gold' is punctuated by the gold deflator label fading slightly — suggesting its irrelevance.

scenes.notes: BRIEF AND PHILOSOPHICAL. This scene should feel like an afterthought — per the script note, 10-15 seconds of actual visual focus on gold. The 1200ms leading break provides transition time. The collapse animation should be fast (30 frames) and dramatic — the opposite of the slow drifts in earlier scenes. All values near zero create a visually flat chart near the bottom — which itself makes the point: gold makes everything look irrelevant. Don't linger. The footnote is dismissive in tone. The punchline 'no one buys eggs with gold' should land during the visual still.
scenes.voiceover: <break time="1200ms"/> And one more lens. Gold. <break time="500ms"/> If you'd measured your groceries against gold's twelve-fold rise over this period... everything collapses toward zero. Eggs, coffee, chips — all on sale. Deep, deep on sale. <break time="500ms"/> But no one buys eggs with gold.

visual.description: Split-screen summary — 4 grouped bar charts in a 2×2 grid. Each chart shows the number of products above/below 1.0 for one deflator. Top-left: 'Median Wage' — 2 red bars (above), 4 green bars (below). Top-right: 'CPI' — 3 red, 3 green. Bottom-left: 'Minimum Wage' — 5 red, 1 green. Bottom-right: 'Gold' — 0 red, 6 green. Each bar chart animates in sequence (10-frame stagger between charts). The bars use Muted Red (#E06070) for above-1.0 and Muted Green (#5BBF8C) for below. Product names labeled on each bar. Common title: 'Same Data. Different Ruler.' in Montserrat Bold 36px. Source: 'BLS, FRED, DOL, LBMA' in Sage Silver, bottom.

scenes.notes: THE VISUAL SUMMARY. This 2×2 grid should be the clearest, most information-dense frame in the video. Each mini-chart is simple: bars going up (red) or down (green) from a baseline. The progression from top-left (2 red) to bottom-left (5 red) visually tells the story of shifting perspectives. Stagger the 4 charts: top-left first, top-right second, bottom-left third (the punch), bottom-right last (the absurdity). 6-frame stagger for bars within each chart, 10-frame stagger between charts. Dot grid background active. The 1000ms break at the end creates space before the final scene.
scenes.voiceover: Same six products. Same twenty-five years. Same Bureau of Labor Statistics data. <break time="500ms"/> Under median wages — four out of six got cheaper. Under CPI — three got more expensive. Under the minimum wage — five out of six. Under gold — everything's a bargain. <break time="1000ms"/> Shrinkflation is real. Your chip bag lost twenty-three percent of its weight. Your coffee can lost more than a third. But the biggest shrinkage isn't in the package. <break time="1000ms"/>

visual.description: Clean dark background (#1A1B22). Text sequence with timed reveals: 1) 'Cheaper for whom?' in Montserrat Bold 56px, Accent Cream, centered (holds for 3s). 2) Fades to: 'Same data. Same math. Different ruler.' in Montserrat 36px (holds for 3s). 3) Below it, 'Different reality.' fades in, slightly larger (40px), with a subtle Muted Pink underline. 4) Final 2 seconds: channel logo (The World With Numbers) fades in below, plus subscribe prompt. End screen compatible — leave right 20% of frame clear for YouTube end screen elements.

sequence.text: Same data. Same math. Different ruler.

scenes.notes: FINAL FRAME. Minimalist. The text sequence should feel deliberate and weighty. Each text element crossfades (8 frames) to the next. 'Cheaper for whom?' echoes the hook's question. 'Different reality.' gets the Muted Pink underline — the only color accent in the scene. Channel logo should be the meridian-line arc logo, small, bottom-center. Subscribe prompt in Inter 18px, Sage Silver. End screen overlay zone: right 20% of frame kept clear per YouTube end screen requirements. Film grain 3%. Hold final frame for 5+ seconds for end screen.
scenes.voiceover: It's in the question we forgot to ask. <break time="500ms"/> Cheaper for whom? <break time="500ms"/> Same data. Same math. Different ruler. <break time="500ms"/> Different reality.
